## The idea

Play C, F, G, C as root-position chords. The harmony is clear and every upper
part jumps with each root. Revoice the same chords so nearby notes stay put or
move by step. The progression becomes four melodies that happen to form chords.

*Voice leading* is the control of those individual lines. A four-note texture can
be stored as soprano, alto, tenor, and bass arrays. A useful first objective is
small total movement, with penalties for crossed voices and rewards for common
tones. The musical problem resembles constrained optimisation more than chord
lookup.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

define :play_lines do |lines, muted|
  lines.each do |name, pitches|
    next if name == muted
    in_thread do
      pitches.each do |pitch|
        play pitch, release: 1.6, amp: 0.55
        sleep 2
      end
    end
  end
  sleep 8
end

naive = {
  bass: [48, 53, 55, 48], tenor: [60, 65, 67, 60],
  alto: [64, 69, 71, 64], soprano: [67, 72, 74, 67]
}

led = {
  bass: [48, 53, 55, 48], tenor: [55, 57, 55, 55],
  alto: [60, 60, 59, 60], soprano: [64, 65, 62, 64]
}

define :movement do |lines|
  lines.values.sum do |pitches|
    pitches.each_cons(2).sum { |a, b| (a - b).abs }
  end
end

puts "naive movement: #{movement(naive)}"
puts "led movement: #{movement(led)}"
play_lines naive, nil
play_lines led, nil
[:bass, :tenor, :alto, :soprano].each { |name| play_lines(led, name) }
```

Both versions spell the same C-F-G-C progression. The second keeps G in the
tenor across several chords and holds C in the alto where possible. Muting one
line changes the texture without changing the remaining data, which makes each
path easier to follow.

## Change one thing

1. Move the led soprano's G-chord note from 62 to 74. One twelve-semitone leap
   raises the objective score and pulls attention away from the other lines.
2. Swap tenor and alto on one chord. The pitch-class collection survives, but
   the voices cross and their identities become harder to trace.
3. Mute each line in turn. Notice which chord loses its root, third, or leading
   tone, and which omission changes the cadence most.

## Why it works

`movement` sums absolute differences between successive pitches in each voice.
It is a cost function, not a complete theory. The lower score corresponds to
smaller steps in this controlled comparison. A fuller search would reject voice
crossing, keep each line inside a range, preserve required chord tones, and
prefer contrary motion at cadences.

Representing lines first changes the architecture. A chord-list model answers
which pitches sound at one time. A voice model also answers where each pitch came
from and where it goes. Transposing the data matrix gives either view.

The greedy voicing from Lesson 27 minimised one transition at a time. A global
search can evaluate the whole progression, because an inexpensive choice now
may force a large leap later. Four voices and a small candidate set remain small
enough for exhaustive enumeration.

Common tones deserve a separate reward even though zero movement already lowers
the cost. Holding a note changes articulation as well as distance: one voice can
sustain through the chord boundary while the others move. The current renderer
reattacks every pitch, hiding that distinction. A later version could merge
equal adjacent events in one line and let the sustained common tone bind the
harmonies together.

## Take it further

Generate every inversion of the four C-F-G-C chords within fixed bass, tenor,
alto, and soprano ranges. Reject crossings and missing chord tones. Score each
complete path by total movement, then play the cheapest path and the root-position
baseline. Your report must print both scores and the four resulting voice arrays.
